sections.body: Course design and teaching is the part of AI research that deals with building and running courses, from writing learning outcomes to marking student work. In practice, AI systems now draft syllabi, generate quiz questions and problem sets, summarise lecture notes into slides, and answer student questions through course-specific tutors. These tools are used by instructors and teaching staff, not as replacements for them, and most deployments stay inside a single course or programme. The work is less about a general teaching machine and more about narrow assistants that handle repetitive preparation and feedback tasks.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Assessment generation is the most mature area, with language models producing multiple choice items, short answer prompts and rubrics that instructors then edit. Personalised learning and early warning systems are further along in prediction than in intervention, since flagging a student at risk is easier than changing what happens next. Course-specific tutors work reasonably well when grounded in a course's own materials, and poorly when asked to answer outside them. The honest limits are real: generated assessments can contain errors, tutors can state wrong facts with confidence, and early warning models can encode bias from past grades. Nothing here is settled enough to run a course without a human reviewing the output.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader starting from scratch should begin with Curriculum and Learning Outcomes, which covers how courses are structured and how outcomes are written before any tool is applied. Generating Assessments then follows the assessment side, covering item writing, rubrics and the quality checks that generated questions need. Personalised Learning and Early Warning takes up the student-facing side, where models track progress and flag difficulty, and it is the page to read for the prediction and bias questions. Course-Specific AI Tutors covers the grounded tutor built on one course's readings, which is where retrieval and scope limits matter most. Lecture Materials from Notes closes the set by covering the conversion of raw notes into slides and handouts, the least glamorous and most immediately useful of the five.
